description: sustainable green marketing and design: system perspective (228 studies) As the largest cluster, with 228 articles, cluster 1 dates back to 1992. These studies investigate different theoretical models to demonstrate the relationships between determinants and the corresponding strategies in this category. The authors found three sub-themes, namely ‘the impact of sustainable green marketing strategy on firm performance,’ ‘sustainable competitive advantages and sustainability strategy,’ and ‘reframing sustainability from the macro-level of system perspective.’ The first sub-theme holds the prime focus of research on the significance of sustainable green marketing strategies in improving sustainable development. A growing number of firms have adopted sustainable green marketing, which has been studied by numerous researchers who embrace green sustainability as a strategic marketing approach (Rivera‐camino 2007; Rudawska 2018). By drawing on system perspectives, these researchers aim at developing a systematic integration of green into a comprehensive marketing strategy through multiple orientations such as planning, functional level, practices, systems, and processes that have significant impacts on corporations, societies, and the global environment. Research is also emerging across other elements of the marketing mix, such as green advertising (Leonidou, Katsikeas, and Morgan 2013) and the whole marketing mix simultaneously (Cronin et al. 2011; Fraj, Martínez, and Matute 2013). The firm performance in turn, achieves significant welfare such as new product success and increased market share from greening the marketing mix process (Ahmed et al. 2019, Leonidou, Katsikeas, and Morgan (2013). In short, this subtheme investigates two main research questions: How can green sustainability be integrated into a comprehensive marketing strategy? and What is the impact of sustainable green marketing strategy on firm performance? The second sub-theme includes articles that view sustainability as a competitive advantage. This perspective is warranted given the rise of responsible and ethical consumers (Connelly, Ketchen, and Slater 2011). From the firm’s perspective, superior performance can be derived from monopoly rents sustained by pioneer market positions (Caves and Porter 1977). Regarding the sources of sustainable competitive advantage (resources and skills such as practices and capability), dominant studies indicate sustainability viewpoints that conceptualize sustainability practices as sustainable innovations (Slager and Chapple 2016), sustainable supply chain management (Maury 2018), sustainable market orientation (Kumar et al. 2011), and sustainable competitive performance (Waheed and Zhang 2020). The underpinning theoretical grounds are comprised of dynamic capability, stakeholder orientation, and market orientation of corporate sustainability (Heikkurinen and Bonnedahl 2013) and the theory of competitive advantages. These studies address challenges and pathways for transforming strategic management paradigms beyond conventional business, thus providing potential resolutions beyond sustainability paradoxes and hindrances to enhance sustainability in the business sector as well as the market. For the sake of generality, the two following research questions have been addressed: (1) What are the competitive advantages associated with the sustainability strategy? (2) Which theoretical perspectives can explain the competitive advantages of the sustainability strategy? The third sub-theme within this category is ‘reframing sustainability from the macro-level of system perspective’ which aims at clarifying which sustainability aspects emerge from the macro-level of system perspective. The majority of studies are concerned with reframing sustainability from the system perspective of the natural environment, institutions, and legitimacy. This means that a complex system is more than a shape or a static configuration of components, making it essential to understand such a system’s self-generating and self-organizing processes (Capra and Luisi 2014). This macro-marketing approach has given rise to increasingly diverse contributions from industryspecific sustainability systems such as luxury fashion (Karaosman et al. 2020; Wong and Ngai 2021) or agriculture (Svensson and Padin 2020) to sustainable thinking for both business and government (Sheth and Parvatiyar 2021), and then to the marketing ecosystem (Waheed and Zhang 2020) of sustainable development based on the invisible hand of market demands. Another issue is a more macro viewpoint focusing on the comprehensive set of antecedents related to institutions and the legitimacy of social sustainability strategies. Thus, components of social sustainability would be institutionalized in law, public discourses, industry norms, or corporate values, ideologies, and policies (Cheah, Low, and Lee 2020; De Clercq, Thongpapanl, and Voronov 2018; Perego and Kolk 2012).

Being the second-largest cluster among the six clusters, with 147 articles, cluster 2’s first publication was in 1994. The sustainability assessment contributes to sustainability and its contextual interpretation (i.e., interpretation challenges of local and global standards) into strategy formulation and decision making by identifying and assessing sustainability objectives, implementations, and outputs. There are three sub-themes within this category, namely ‘the impact of corporate environmental disclosure on performance,’ ‘the influence of CSR disclosure on firm performance,’ and ‘the impact of sustainability reporting/corporate sustainability disclosure on performance.’ This cluster focuses mainly on different types of sustainability information such as environmental issues, environmental emissions, and social information that typically includes community and employee metrics and comprehensive sustainability disclosure indicators/indices. A series of research questions have been addressed, including: (1) What are negative consequences of low transparent corporate environmental disclosure? (2) Is there a positive relationship between CSR disclosure and economic performance? (3) What aspects are covered in a comprehensive sustainability report? (4) Are there disparities in the content of sustainability reports across different governance and firm characteristics? The first sub-theme is related to the impact of corporate environmental disclosure on performance. This delivers various findings, depending on the theoretical perspectives taken. The first argument relies on corporate managers and social concerns (Aerts, Cormier, and Magnan 2008), and media attention (Haddock‐Fraser and Fraser 2008), which is a function of social and political pressures to gain legitimacy for stakeholders. Thus, low-environment-performance companies tend to publish unmaintainable details to change public images. Conversely, firms with lower transparency information and corporate governance (Choi et al. 2019; Jacoby et al. 2019), face information risks (Jacoby et al. 2019) Regarding the second sub-theme, prevailing studies conceptualize CSR disclosure as social information reporting and/or CSR reports. The aspect of this sub-theme focuses on the link between CSR and economic performance. These typical studies deliberate on the nature of CSR actions, from the perspective of CSR disclosure, which indirectly/ directly contribute to the firm’s profitability such as in the stock market, market-based firm value (Menz 2010; Nekhili et al. 2017), and business performance (Nekhili et al. 2017). In addition, firms use social and environmental disclosure to signal their commitment to external stakeholders (i.e., capital markets) as well as to differentiate themselves from competitors. The third sub-theme is related to the emerging sustainability disclosure and Environmental, Social, and Corporate Governance (ESG) information. This sub-theme, in short, is related to combining issues on a company’s environmental, social, and governance disclosure or annual reporting. Regarding theoretical approaches, the stakeholder approach and signaling perspective highlight corporate use of voluntary disclosure to raise their concerns and notify stakeholders of sustainability-related issues. Additionally, the impact of community concerns is also covered as measured by the extent of media attention on social and environmental disclosure (Deegan, Rankin, and Tobin 2002) and the state-of-the-art environmental and social reporting of UK firms (Gray, Kouhy, and Lavers 1995). Furthermore, ESG information is another non-financial metric becoming increasingly prominent in many countries (Vives and Wadhwa 2012), being hailed overwhelmingly as the triple bottom line approach promoting economic, ecological, and social-ethical development (Dyllick and Hockerts 2002). The detailed level and disclosure quality of sustainability reporting each vary across different firm characteristics (e.g., family firms vs. public ones) as well as governance characteristics (e.g., corporate governance and board composition). As with environmental and social factors, these studies show that when delivering ecological and social information, the governance dimension is incorporated as a proper governance structure that positively contributes to firms’ profitability and efficient allocation of capital to the ecosystem and society with the voluntary disclosure (Fabrizio and Kim 2019). Other issues are emerging, such as environmental risk management (Muhammad et al. 2015), sustainability metrics (Consolandi et al. 2009), and sustainable finance (Soppe 2004).

Being the newest cluster with 103 articles, cluster 3 gained its first publication in 2004. This third research agenda reconciles the comprehension of a system model that combines trends in social sustainability literature and the interdisciplinary endeavor (multiple views) on different levels for the model-based development. There are, in detail, three themes within the category: ‘motivations and outcomes of social sustainability,’ ‘mediators (e.g., marketing competence) and moderators (e.g., market environment) of the relationship between social sustainability and firm performance,’ and ‘the stakeholder concept: supply chain CSR (from multidiscipline).’ Regarding the first sub-theme, most of the studies in this cluster are devoted to dynamic models of social sustainability with two primary levels of complexity. From the mechanism in systems orientation (causes and effects), the simple research models either study the antecedents or outcomes of CSR, whereas the more complicated models integrate both antecedents and outcomes and incorporate mediators, moderators, or both. The simplest model is the model with antecedents and social sustainability, including studies of Jahdi and Acikdilli (2009), Flammer (2015), Homburg, Stierl, and Bornemann (2013), Luo and Bhattacharya (2009). Those antecedents are stakeholders’ relations in the context of shareholders, consumers, market competition, and certification demands (Aguinis and Glavas 2012). The antecedents can be divided into three groups in order of overall prominence among the articles, such as firm driving factors (based on resource-based view, social contract theory, stakeholder theory, resource dependence), demands from other stakeholders (stakeholder theory, socialization theory) and contextual factors (institutional theory, stakeholder theory, and agency theory) (Du et al. 2013; Nikolaeva and Bicho 2011). From the second mechanism in systems orientation (effects), another straightforward model accompanies outcomes demonstrated in the papers of Luo and Bhattacharya (2006), Luo and Bhattacharya (2009), and Homburg, Stierl, and Bornemann (2013). In relation to the consequences/outcomes of social sustainability strategy, two categories are discovered. The initial group of outcomes is related to performance, grouped into two categories: firm value-market value and product market performance. Moreover, other outcomes in order of prominence included financial outcomes such as cost/ risk (firm-idiosyncratic risks), and profits/sales,

which are a proxy for the financial performance effect used to analyze forecasts. Additionally, the relationships between CSR practices and employee performance (Du, Bhattacharya, and Sen 2015) and competitive performance (such as customer satisfaction) from a multistakeholder perspective are investigated. Employee performance is also classified into CSR involvement, organizational attachment and organizational citizenship behaviors (Du, Bhattacharya, and Sen 2015). Three main research questions have been examined in this sub-theme: (1) What are the reasons behind the adoption of social sustainability? (2) Do they depend on different theoretical perspectives? and (3) What are the benefits and costs of adopting social sustainability? The second dynamic model is where scholars have investigated mediators such as marketing competence and moderators such as market environment and show why CSR have various effects on corporate outcomes (Bai and Chang 2015). Also, from a micro-level perspective, Hoang, Bui Thanh, and Palazzo (2021) found that relationship marketing orientation as an opportunity moderates social sustainability-firm performance outcomes. Correspondingly, the research by Leonidou, Katsikeas, and Morgan (2013) indicates that corporate privileges are achieved via sustainable green marketing tactics. The further development of the existing frameworks is indicated in the literature of competitive and sustainable advantages; thus, a range of new mediators and moderators such as market turbulence, marketing competence, new product success, and product quality (Ahmed et al. 2019; Bai and Chang 2015) are drawn into the portrayal. As such, the authors are beginning to achieve a grip on these complicated networks, such as the competitive advantage of external stakeholders (customer satisfaction) (Hsu 2012; Korschun, Bhattacharya, and Swain 2014; Lai et al. 2010; Luo and Zhang 2016), and the competitive advantage of internal stakeholders (transactional leadership, organization trust) (Hansen et al. 2011; Mishra and Modi 2016; Saeidi et al. 2015). In short, this subtheme helps clarify the question, what are the dynamic mechanisms connecting social sustainability and firm performance? The final sub-theme within cluster 3 is the ‘The stakeholder concept: supply chain CSR (from multi-discipline) that aims to investigate, how is supply chain CSR conceptualized from the stakeholder perspective? In detail, stakeholder theories can be divided into normative, descriptive, and instrumental perspectives (Donaldson and Preston 1995). The descriptive stakeholder theory attempts to show the actual relationship between managers and their stakeholders empirically. The other two perspectives explain the relationship between stakeholder management and the achievement of traditional objectives (e.g., profitability, growth). The normative stakeholder theory reflects the relationship between the identification of moral or philosophical guidelines for the operation and management of corporations (Donaldson and Preston 1995). A picture of social sustainability and marketing can be obtained by using a conceptual framework such as the framework of CSR in marketing (Vaaland, Heide, and Grønhaug 2008) and the integrative stakeholder framework in marketing (Maignan and Ferrell 2004).

First published in 1994, this cluster is comprised of 91 studies in total. The publications mainly adopt the established literature from general management and focus on the connection between social sustainability/corporate sustainability and different management levels. There are two main subthemes within the category, including ‘the relationship between strategic social sustainability and performance management’ and ‘corporate sustainability integration and sustainability performance.’ Three main research questions have been examined in this cluster: (1) How is strategic social sustainability leading firms to manage their performance effectively? (2) What are the measurement dimensions of firm performance? and (3) To what extent sustainability being integrated at both strategic and operational levels can ensure the achievement of strategic sustainability goals? Concerning the first sub-theme, the relationship between strategic CSR and performance is generally not likely to be direct or straightforward, but rather moderated by firm contingency (Yin and Jamali 2016) and mediated by shared values (Kelley, Hemphill, and Thams 2019). Stakeholder perspective (Orlitzky 2013) and the configurational 12 L. PHAN TAN ET AL. approach of strategic social sustainability (the pattern of strategic social sustainability practices) (Kelley, Hemphill, and Thams 2019) are prevailing theoretical approaches used to explain the motivations that corporates apply to social sustainability strategy. In addition, based on the second viewpoint, strategic social sustainability has been used to predict value creation-firm and social value (Yin and Jamali 2016), performance-financial performance and non-financial performance (Lopez, Fornes, and Juan Carlos Sosa Varela 2015), and employee outcomes (Holmqvist 2009). Furthermore, social sustainability creates signals to incentivize employee performance, behavior, and work-site health promotion regarding employee-related outcomes. Regarding financial outcomes, long-term financial performance (Lopez, Fornes, and Juan Carlos Sosa Varela 2015), firm value (Yin and Jamali 2016), marketoriented (stock market volatility) (Orlitzky 2013), and marketing performance measured by market share (Rahman, Rodríguez-Serrano, and Lambkin 2017) have been studied. The second sub-theme is related to corporate sustainability integration through which holistic corporate activities at both strategic and operational levels are required to implement sustainable performance management guidelines and successfully reach strategic sustainability goals. The underpinning theoretical drivers include dynamic capability, stakeholder orientation, and market orientation that determine corporate sustainability (Heikkurinen and Bonnedahl 2013) or sustainability agency in stakeholder management (Romestant 2020).

With its initial study taking place in 1997, cluster 5 is the second smallest, achieving 28 studies. This cluster highlights the effects of environmental and social practices on economic performance. There are three sub-themes in this cluster: ‘the impact of environmental sustainability management on economic sustainability,’ ‘the influence of social sustainability management on economic sustainability,’ and ‘the operationalization of sustainability strategies.’ This cluster addresses five main research questions: (1) What is the emerging conceptualization of environmental sustainability management? (2) Does the passive or proactive management perspective affect economic sustainability? (3) What does social sustainability management mean? (4) Does social sustainability management influence economic sustainability? (5) How do sustainability strategies operate/manifest? Initially, the typical studies in the first sub-theme conceptualize environmental sustainability as global environmental standards (Dowell, Hart, and Yeung 2000) and environmental practice integration and strategy (Kotler 2011; Maxwell et al. 1997; Wagner 2007). Several studies, in turn, propose the impact of environmental management on economic performance, but they are grounded in passive compliance of environmental sustainability in prior studies (legitimacy perspective) and arguments of sustainability advantage through altruistic liability or value-added assets (Dowell, Hart, and Yeung 2000), proactive engagement environmental strategies (Maxwell et al. 1997), and strategic environmental management literature (Wagner 2007). These emerging concepts shift attention from management commitments (Maxwell et al. 1997) to environmental management integration with economic aspects and balanced scorecard tools (Wagner 2007) to gain significant impacts on corporations, society, and economic performance. This framework study indicates obstacles and pathways for evolving from a strategic environmental management paradigm shift to more potential resolutions beyond environmental sustainability paradoxes. Regarding the second sub-theme, the dominant studies explicitly link social sustainability, marketing strategy, innovation, and economic performance. Social sustainability management consists of the co-creation process of upstream social sustainability (innovative fair-trade schemes) and downstream (responsible consumers) through identification and trust (He and Harris 2020; Padgett and Galan 2010) in the achievement of traditional objectives (e.g., profitability, growth) and community advantage (Quazi and O’brien 2000). Social responsibility has been studied as CSR actions (Murray and Vogel 1997) or corporate social performances (McWilliams and Siegel 2000), JOURNAL OF BUSINESS-TO-BUSINESS MARKETING 13 which indirectly/directly contribute to financial performance and firm outcomes. Regarding the third sub-theme, dominant studies indicate three sustainability viewpoints that conceptualize sustainability strategies such as sustainable practices (Ameer and Othman 2012), sustainable innovations (Nakata and Viswanathan 2012), and sustainable market orientation (Viswanathan et al. 2009). The further underpinning theoretical grounds are dynamic capacity and the base of the pyramid (BOP) for social innovation (Nakata and Viswanathan 2012), multidimensional perspectives based on economic/ environmental/social indicators of sustainable practices (Ameer and Othman 2012), and bottomup orientation corporate sustainability in subsistence marketplaces (Viswanathan et al. 2009). This cluster thus filled the gap between the forces of economic sustainability and social sustainability/ environmental sustainability and emerging integration concepts. The simultaneous interrelated relationships of all three aspects of sustainability and social sustainability integration based on stakeholder models are still overlooked. Alongside theoretical construct evolution, these studies focus on the context that links environmental sustainability or social sustainability or sustainable strategy with economic sustainability, innovation, and market strategy.

This is the smallest with six articles, the first of which was published in 1995 linked in a more or less direct way to environmental and natural resources protection. Within the category, these studies investigate, in the broad perspective, what are the environmental sustainability and green practices of multinational enterprises? and how do these practices influence financial performance? The majority of studies indicated that various endogenous factors – such as tangibility of sector, firm size, innovative orientation, family influence, and perceived financial benefits from energy conservation – predict an enterprises’ level of engagement in selected environmental management practices, which involve monitoring of company waste, and the producing or selling of environmentally friendly products. In addition, these studies emphasize that high polluting firms (i.e., the world’s major oil multinationals), therefore, face an obligation from regulation and consumer pressures to spend more on abatement as framed by the regulatory settings (Pulver 2007) or public concerns (boycotting). Two articles refer to corporations enhancing competitive advantage, costsaving and market share to gain financial performance from environmental practices (Klassen and McLaughlin 1996; Menguc and Ozanne 2005). The latter focused on these corporations to enhance a better understanding of what drives multinational enterprises to engage in environmental practices and whether the drivers differ across the types of practices such as operating activities. This minority study aims at identifying why such particular organizations decide to go green to understand the particular motives of ecological responsiveness in such firms. Three main drivers, including legitimation (stakeholder pressure), competitiveness (strategic and economic benefits), and social responsibility, have been identified. These findings are also corroborated by Nejati, Amran, and Ahmad (2014), who studied the relationship between stakeholders’ influences and environmental responsibility. These authors emphasized two types of stakeholders – employees and customers – as those significantly influence environmental responsibilities, which then result in financial improvements. This cluster highlights the transformation of the environmental sustainability concept from a legitimate perspective to cultural orientation issues deserving senior management and company attention.
